text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden's Supreme Court will review a case about whether car manufacturers or car owners should pay car repairs needed for cars that have too high levels of emissions. If car producers are found to be financially responsible for the repairs, they may have to pay expensive engine repairs for tens of thousands of car owners.

- When Education & Science Minister Carl Tham wrote a column in the newspaper on January 29 saying he was against Swedish membership in Europe's monetary union (EMU), it caused large irritation among other ministers, newspaper sources say. Ministers in the minority Social Democratic government are supposed to keep a low profile in the EMU issue and not disturb discussions at party grass root levels.

- Carl Bildt, international mediator to Bosnia and the leader of the Swedish conservatives, the Moderate Party, will go to Washington on Wednesday to see U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Clinton's security advisor Sandy Berger.

- About ten of Swedish electricity intensive companies could get cuts in the so called production tax on electricity, Prime Minister Goran Persson told a seminar in northern Sweden on Tuesday. At the same seminar, Industry and Commerce Minister Anders Sundstrom promised to allocate 300 million crowns to develop the Swedish forestry industry.
- Union members of company boards are loyal to company owners rather than to staff, a study at Lund University shows.
- Swedish telecoms group Ericsson showed a continued high rate of growth by posting a record 1996 pretax profit of more than ten billion crowns.
- The Swedish competition authority raided the two largest domestic boat equipment wholesale firms early on Tuesday following suspicions of illegal price cooperation.

- Spurred by European Union requirements to spread their risks, Sweden's financial institutions are investing heavily in foreign bonds. Swedish firms last year purchased 48 billion crowns worth of foreign bonds, the largest amount ever in a single year.

- In an effort to turn back the tide of falling profits, Volvo Trucks this year has embarked upon a major drive to cut costs which is to be completed this year. Volvo Truck's target is to reduce annual costs by a minimum of three to four billion crowns, newspaper sources say.

- AB LM Ericsson, the world's largest supplier of telecommunications equipment, reported on Tuesday that its pre-tax profit climbed by 33 percent to 10.1 billion crowns, a result which was roughly in line with market expectations.
